children.text: Lumbar spinal stenosis is a degenerative spinal condition characterized by the narrowing of the lumbar spinal canal due to a variety of bony or soft tissue structures
Diagnosis is made with MRI of the lumbar spine

Treatment is a trial of nonoperative management with NSAIDs and physical therapy. Surgical laminotomy and discectomy are indicated for progressive disabling pain and/or progressive neurological deficits that have failed nonoperative management
most common reason for lumbar spine surgery in patients >65 y/o
average age at presentation is 65 y/o
failure of posterior elements to develop, leading to short pedicles and laminae
Narrowing of the lumbar spinal canal can be due to
hypertrophy or buckling of the **ligamentum flavum**
cell, water, and proteoglycan content in the nucleus pulposus decrease with age
degeneration of the intervertebral disk leads to diminished disk height and buckling/bulging of the annulus fibrosus
**anterior spinal column begins to have decreased ability to absorb stress, leading to an abnormal transfer of force to the posterior elements**
increased stress through the facets leads to facet joint hypertrophy, osteophyte formation, and ligamentum flavum buckling and hypertrophy
combined changes lead to a narrowing of the spinal canal and compression of the neural elements
project posteriorly from posterolateral corners of vertebral bodies
project posteromedially from the pedicles and join in the midline
project posteriorly from superior articular facet
mass of bone between superior and inferior articular facets
act as articulations above and below
formed by superior and inferior articular processes that project from junction of pedicle and lamina
nerve root exits in the foramen under same-numbered pedicle
central herniations affect traversing nerve root
far lateral herniations affect exiting nerve root
dorsal branches supply blood to the dura & posterior elements
secondary to systemic diseases (Paget disease, acromegaly, and fluorosis)
short pedicles with medially placed facets
cross-sectional area <100 mm² or <10 mm anteroposterior diameter on axial CT
caused by ligamentum hypertrophy directly under the lamina posteriorly and the bulging disc anteriorly
presents with symptoms of nonspecific root or lower nerve root compression (at the L4-5 level, the root of L5 is affected)
caused by facet joint arthropathy and osteophyte formation
overgrowth of the superior articular facet is usually the primary culprit
presents with symptoms of **descending nerve root** compression (at the L4-5 level, the root of L5 is affected)
occurs between the medial and lateral borders of the pedicle
caused by a substantial loss of disc height, foraminal disc protrusion or osteophytes, or angulation in the setting of degenerative scoliosis
results in nerve root compression by the ventral cephalad overhang of the superior facet and the bulging disc
presents with symptoms of **exiting nerve root** compression (at the L4-5 level, the root of L4 is affected)
located lateral to the lateral edge of the pedicle
caused by far lateral disc herniation
presents with symptoms of **exiting nerve root** compression (at the L4-5 level, the root of L4 is affected)
pain worse with extension (walking or standing upright)
pain relieved with flexion (sitting, leaning over shopping cart, or sleeping in the fetal position)
recurrent UTIs present in up to 10% due to autonomic sphincter dysfunction
unilateral radicular pain from foraminal stenosis made worse by back extension
radicular pain is not worsened by the Valsalva maneuver, unlike in a herniated disc
patients may have no focal deficits, as exam often takes place with the patient seated and symptoms may be reproducible or exacerbated only with lumbar extension or ambulation
findings do not always correlate with clinical symptomatology
nonspecific degenerative findings (disc space narrowing, osteophyte formation)
segmental instability and subtle degenerative spondylolisthesis
plain-film myelography provides dynamic information such as degree of cut off when a patient goes into extension
central stenosis with a thecal sac <100 mm²
obliteration of perineural fat and compression of lateral recess or foramen
MRI findings of spinal stenosis may be found in asymptomatic patients
central and lateral neural element compression
Important to differentiate symptoms of neurogenic claudication from those of vascular claudication
flexion improves symptoms in neurogenic claudication because this posture increases the limited area available for the neural elements in the spinal canal and foramen
presence of coexisting hip and spine pathology
must determine the primary pain generator prior to surgical treatment
may require diagnostic injections to aid in diagnosis
oral medications, physical therapy, and corticosteroid injections
NSAIDs, physical therapy, weight loss, and bracing
preoperative opioid use associated with prolonged hospital stays and increased postoperative pain
have been found to be effective and may obviate the need for surgery
persistent pain for 3-6 months that has failed to improve with nonoperative management
results in greater improvement in pain and function than nonsurgical treatment
wide pedicle-to-pedicle decompression with instrumented fusion
segmental instability (isthmic spondylolisthesis, degenerative spondylolisthesis, degenerative scoliosis)
created by complete laminectomy and/or removal of >50% of facets
risk of adjacent segment degeneration >30% at 10 years
a single level decompression at L4-5 would include
resection of the inferior half of the spinous process of L4
resection of the L4 lamina to the level of the insertion of the ligamentum flavum
medial facetectomy and lateral recess decompression
undercutting of the facets and removal of ligamentum flavum from lateral recess
exploration and decompression of the L4-5 and L5-S1 foramina
palpate the L4 and L5 pedicle (pedicle-to-pedicle) and be sure the nerve root is patent below it
**improved pain, function, and satisfaction with surgical treatment**
most common cause of failed surgery is **recurrence of disease** above or below the decompressed level
comorbid conditions are the strongest predictor of clinical outcomes after decompression for lumbar spinal stenosis
circumferential fusion (with PLIF or TLIF) is accepted, but no studies show its superiority
Complications increase with age, blood loss, and levels fused
deep surgical infections are to be treated with surgical debridement and irrigation
genitofemoral nerve deficits are common following a transpsoas approach at higher lumbar levels
femoral and/or obturator nerve is at risk with prolonged or excessive retraction during a transpsoas approach to the L4-L5 disc space
